passage:
"Baba, why do birds fly in a V?" said Payal, standing beside the desk.
"Hmm?" said Amandeep, eyes on the laptop. "Something about air. I'll tell you later."
"And why does the moon follow the car?"
"It doesn't, really."
"But why does it seem to?"
"Payal, I'm working."
"Baba, why is your screen bright?"
Amandeep stopped typing and looked at Payal. "You're asking a lot of questions. Are they about the birds, or about me?"
Payal shrugged, and said softly, "I don't want you to look at the laptop."
"Okay. Give me ten minutes, then I'm all yours."

qa.q: What did Payal ask about birds?
qa.a: Why birds fly in a V.

qa.q: What was Payal really wanting when asking about the bright screen?
qa.a: Payal felt ignored and wanted Baba's attention, softly saying, 'I don't want you to look at the laptop.'

qa.q: What small step helped Payal and Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep noticed the need for connection and promised a set time to give full attention after finishing the work.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have felt when Payal said "I don't want you to look at the laptop"?
qa.a: Touched and a bit guilty, realising the questions were about connection, so Amandeep stopped typing and promised ten minutes.

grounding: A child asks many questions to keep an adult engaged rather than because of the topic, and noticing the need for connection reduces the pressure.

passage: My name is Nirmala. When I was nine, I used to follow Nani Sudha around the kitchen asking things. "Why does rice swell? Where does steam go? Why is the pot black?" I didn't really care about the answers. Nani would answer patiently and keep chopping. One day she put down the knife, wiped her hands and looked at me. "Nirmala, I think you want me to stay with you. Is that right?" My face went hot, but I nodded. She smiled, pulled up a stool and said, "Come, tell me about your day, and I'll chop and listen." That afternoon I stopped asking about steam and talked about my friend's lost pencil box.

qa.q: Whose kitchen did Nirmala follow Nani Sudha around?
qa.a: Nani Sudha's kitchen.

qa.q: What was Nirmala really feeling when asking about rice and steam?
qa.a: Mostly a wish for Nani's company rather than the answers; when Nani named it, Nirmala's face went hot with embarrassment.

qa.q: What did Nani Sudha do that changed the pattern?
qa.a: Nani put down the knife, named that Nirmala might want company, and invited Nirmala to talk about the day while chopping.

qa.q: How might Nani Sudha have seen the questions before noticing?
qa.a: As ordinary curiosity, answered patiently, until Nani realised they were a way to stay close.

grounding: A child asks many questions to keep an adult engaged, not because of the topic, and the adult responds to the need for connection.

passage:
When I was eight, my big sister Ishita didi was studying for her board exams. I kept going into her room. "Didi, why is the sky blue? Didi, what's the biggest animal? Didi, how do planes stay up?" I didn't care about the answers. I just wanted her to look at me.
She kept saying, "Manjula, I'm studying." Then I'd ask another one.
One evening she put her pen down. She said, "You're asking a lot of questions. Do you just miss me?" I nodded. I felt a bit silly.
She said, "Okay. Every evening at seven, I'll take a ten-minute break, and we'll play something. Deal?" I said deal.
After that, I stopped interrupting. I waited for seven o'clock. We played carrom mostly.

qa.q: What time did Ishita didi take her break?
qa.a: At seven, every evening.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling while asking so many questions?
qa.a: Manjula felt lonely and missed Ishita didi, wanting attention more than answers.

qa.q: What did Ishita didi do that helped?
qa.a: She noticed the need for connection behind the questions and offered a daily ten-minute break to play together.

qa.q: How did Ishita didi feel before she put her pen down?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated and distracted, trying to study with constant interruptions.

grounding: Shows a child asking many questions to keep an older sibling engaged, and the sibling noticing the need for connection.

passage:
Class 4 teacher's note, Friday.
Devika (9) asks a lot of questions at the end of every lesson, when the others are packing up. Today: "Ma'am, why did the Mughals build forts? Ma'am, what's your favourite fort? Ma'am, do you have a dog?" Most are not about the lesson. She stands close and watches my face.
Her mother told me at the parents' meeting that she has a new baby brother at home. I think Devika is looking for a bit of one-on-one attention.
So I've asked her to be my "class helper" on Mondays and Thursdays, collecting books with me after class. Lakshmi will help on the other days. Today, when I told her, Devika beamed and asked only one question: "Can I start Monday?"

qa.q: What new family member does Devika have?
qa.a: A new baby brother at home.

qa.q: What did Devika want from all her questions?
qa.a: She seemed to feel a bit left out at home and was looking for one-on-one attention and connection.

qa.q: What did the teacher do next, and why might it help?
qa.a: She made Devika a class helper twice a week, giving her regular one-on-one time so she doesn't need to ask so many questions.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi feel about being a helper too?
qa.a: Lakshmi would probably feel pleased and included.

grounding: Shows a child asking many questions to keep a teacher engaged, and the teacher noticing the need for connection and responding to it.

passage:
Saturday
Mridul bhaiya was playing a video game all afternoon. I kept asking him questions. "What level are you on? Why is that monster green? Who made this game? What's your favourite level?"
He answered some, then said, "Gautam, why so many questions? You don't even play this."
I didn't know what to say. Then I said, "I just want to hang out."
He paused the game. Looked at me. Then he said, "Okay. One more level, then carrom?"
We played carrom for an hour. He let me win once, I think. I didn't ask a single question the whole time.
Gautam

qa.q: What game did Mridul bhaiya offer after one more level?
qa.a: Carrom.

qa.q: What was Gautam really feeling when asking about the video game?
qa.a: Gautam felt lonely and wanted to spend time with Mridul bhaiya, more than learn about the game.

qa.q: What did Mridul bhaiya do that met Gautam's real need?
qa.a: He noticed the questions weren't about the game, paused, and offered to play carrom together.

qa.q: How might Mridul bhaiya have felt when Gautam said he wanted to hang out?
qa.a: He probably felt touched and a little surprised, which is why he paused the game.

grounding: Shows a child asking many questions to keep an older cousin engaged, and the cousin noticing the need for connection.

passage: In the sugarcane field behind their house near Karnal, Baljeet was fixing the tubewell pipe. Jagdish, nine, squatted beside him. "Bapu, why is the pipe blue?" "It came like that." "Why is the water cold?" "It comes from deep down." "Why is deep down cold? Why do crows sit on the wire? Why—" Baljeet noticed that Jagdish wasn't even looking at the crows. He was looking at his father. Since the baby came, Baljeet realised, he had barely had an evening alone with the boy. He put the spanner down. "Jagdish, want to hold the pipe while I tighten it? I need a helper." Jagdish shot up. For twenty minutes he held the pipe, asked almost nothing, and just grinned.

qa.q: What was Baljeet fixing?
qa.a: He was fixing the tubewell pipe.

qa.q: What did Jagdish really want as he asked question after question?
qa.a: He seemed to want his father's attention and closeness, perhaps feeling left out since the baby came, more than answers about crows.

qa.q: What did Baljeet try, and why did it work?
qa.a: He made Jagdish his helper, which met the need for time together, so the questions faded 🙂

qa.q: What did Baljeet realise while Jagdish kept asking?
qa.a: He realised Jagdish was looking at him, not the crows, and that since the baby came he had hardly had an evening alone with the boy.

grounding: Shows a child asking endless questions to keep a parent engaged, and the parent noticing the need for connection and meeting it.
